setupSteps: Floor and mat: lie on a non-slip mat or carpet on a firm floor. Avoid a soft bed, which lets the back sink and hides the arch.
Noise: the movement is quiet. Place the mat away from the wall so the arms can reach overhead.

Lie on your back: head resting on the floor in a neutral position, eyes on the ceiling. Do not tuck the chin hard or lift the head (a sport-performance source warns that watching your legs strains the neck).
Arms: reach both arms straight up over the chest with the palms facing each other (Fit & Well, MyFitnessPal and Healthline all describe this start).

Legs, full and heel-tap start (tabletop): lift both legs so the hips and knees are bent at about 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor and knees stacked over the hips (Physitrack and other guides). Beginner start: keep both feet flat on the floor with knees bent (the easier start used for the arms-only version).

Check the lower back: slide a hand under the small of the back. You should feel light contact, not a big gap (Fit & Well suggests a neutral spine with a slight natural curve; other sources say press the lower back down). Pick one cue and keep it: FitPlate uses "belly in, lower back stays heavy on the floor".
Brace: breathe out and draw the lower ribs down towards the hips (the "ribs down" cue). Keep that feeling while you move.
Clothing: fitted top and leggings or track pants so the camera can see the hips, knees and shoulders. Loose kurtas hide the hip line.
Water: keep a bottle nearby; this is light work but slow reps feel long.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Lie down and set the start
steps.action: Lie on the mat, arms straight up, knees bent with feet flat (or in tabletop if comfortable).
steps.feel: Back of the head and ribs resting on the floor; calm belly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders, ribs and hips all touching the floor, lower back close to the mat. Front: arms straight up, shoulders level.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Brace the belly
steps.action: Breathe out and gently pull the lower ribs towards the hips so the lower back presses lightly to the floor.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs do not point to the ceiling.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Lower one arm back slowly
steps.action: Keeping the elbow straight, lower the right arm behind your head, stopping before the ribs flare or the lower back lifts.
steps.feel: Stretch in the front of the shoulder; belly working harder to hold the back down.
steps.breathing: Breathe in as the arm lowers (Fit & Well and others suggest in as limbs reach; any steady pattern is fine, never hold the breath).
steps.visualCheck: Side: lower back stays on the floor; ribs stay down. Front: the other arm still straight up, shoulders level.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Return the arm
steps.action: Bring the arm back up over the chest in a controlled arc.
steps.visualCheck: Arm ends straight up over the shoulder, back still flat.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Switch arms
steps.feel: Same even work in both sides.
steps.visualCheck: Pelvis does not tilt or twist.

steps.part: A. Arms-only dead bug (beginner main version)
steps.title: Finish the set
steps.action: Lower both arms and rest your feet or knees.
steps.visualCheck: Stop the set early if the lower back lifted.

steps.part: B. Heel-tap dead bug (beginner step up)
steps.title: Start in tabletop with arms straight up and the lower back lightly pressed down, as in Setup (steps 4-7)

steps.part: B. Heel-tap dead bug (beginner step up)
steps.title: Breathe out to brace, then slowly lower the right heel towards the floor, keeping the knee bent at about 90 degrees (Healthline describes this as keeping the knee bent and tapping the heel to the floor). Breathe in while lowering

steps.part: B. Heel-tap dead bug (beginner step up)
steps.title: Tap the heel lightly or hover it, without letting the lower back arch. Stop earlier if the back lifts

steps.part: B. Heel-tap dead bug (beginner step up)
steps.title: Bring the knee back to tabletop over the hip, breathing out. Repeat with the left. About 3 seconds down, 3 seconds up (est.)

steps.part: B. Heel-tap dead bug (beginner step up)
steps.title: Keep arms up and still in this version, or add arms once your back stays down
Start in tabletop with arms straight up. Brace
Slowly lower the right arm overhead and straighten the left leg away at the same moment, stopping both a few centimetres above the floor, with the lower back still down

Return both to the start together, then repeat on the other side. Breathe in as the limbs reach and out as they return, or out on the reach; pick one and keep it steady (sources differ; see section 7)
Stop the set when the lower back lifts or the ribs flare

commonMistakes.title: Lower back arching off the floor
commonMistakes.text: Lower back arching off the floor. Why: the most-cited error; it lets the hip flexors and back muscles do the work instead of the abs and can aggravate back pain. Fix: shorten the reach, raise the legs, or go back to arms-only or heel taps; keep ribs down.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing
commonMistakes.text: Rushing. Why: fast reps lose control and pull the back off the floor (MyFitnessPal and others). Fix: count 3 s out, 3 s back (est.).

commonMistakes.title: Ribs flaring as the arm goes overhead
commonMistakes.text: Ribs flaring as the arm goes overhead. Why: the ribcage lifts and drags the back into an arch. Fix: stop the arm where the ribs stay down; breathe out to draw the ribs in.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding raises blood pressure more than open breathing during effort (lab data from heavy lifting, PubMed 7741618). Fix: breathe steadily; exhale with effort.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the head or tucking the chin to watch the legs
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the head or tucking the chin to watch the legs. Why: strains the neck. Fix: eyes on the ceiling, head resting.

commonMistakes.title: Legs too low or straightened too far too soon
commonMistakes.text: Legs too low or straightened too far too soon. Why: a long lever arm lifts the back. Fix: keep knees bent (heel taps) until the back stays flat.

commonMistakes.title: Pelvis tipping or hips rocking
commonMistakes.text: Pelvis tipping or hips rocking. Why: the spine moves instead of resisting. Fix: move one limb pair slowly with a still pelvis.

commonMistakes.title: Bulging or coning in the middle of the belly (mostly postpartum)
commonMistakes.text: Bulging or coning in the middle of the belly (mostly postpartum). Why: a sign of poor pressure control. Fix: shorten the range, exhale earlier, and ask a physiotherapist.

safetyNotes: Back problems: commonly used as a low-load back exercise, but stay in a range where the back does not arch or hurt; a small group of people find most exercise, including the dead bug, aggravates their pain. Stop if the pain rises.
Neck or shoulder problems: limit the arm range; keep the head resting.
High blood pressure and heart disease: breathe steadily, avoid breath-holding, get up slowly from the floor; get clearance for severe or uncontrolled BP or known heart disease.

Pregnancy and postpartum: the exercise is done lying on the back; guidelines advise limiting back-lying after the first trimester or after 20 weeks (sources disagree); ask an obstetrician. After childbirth, check for abdominal separation first and stop if the belly bulges or domes.
Recent surgery (especially abdominal), dizziness or balance problems on the floor: only with approval.
Osteoporosis: the dead bug avoids spinal flexion (practitioner sources), but a clinician should confirm the right exercises for you.
